transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Kim (Redwood SE), Tom Reynolds (Empiria SRE), Leila Ortiz (Empiria Product), Samir Gupta (Empiria SecOps)

Auto summary: Jordan runs through the console trace playback and shows a real-world example of a cached KV miss leading to a downstream model fallback. Tom asks for retention and audit detail. Maya clarifies pricing/commit implications for Dedicated.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you making time. quick intro, im maya patel, I'll own the account and jordan's gonna run the technical bits today.
[00:17] Tom: thanks, yeah, we've been seeing intermittent 95th percentile spikes on our chat endpoint, so the SRE team wants to walk through how we'd debug that with your console.
[00:28] Jordan: great, perfect — we'll start with request inspector, then trace playback, then error forensics and runbook. I have a short demo trace that mimics what you sent earlier — names sanitized.
[00:44] Leila: quick Q, is this the same console we've been poking at in the eval tenant? or is this a dedicated view?
[00:51] Jordan: good Q — this is console-hosted view with sample traces from Hosted. If you go Dedicated, the UI is the same, but you get additional per-token cost telemetry and segregation in the dashboard.
[01:05] Samir: and for VPC/onprem we still see the request playback? any difference?
[01:11] Jordan: you still get the trace events; in Private deployment we redact customer PII by default and we integrate with their KMS for key ops. But the playback artifacts are the same.
[01:24] [Jordan screenshare: console, request inspector list]
[01:28] Jordan: here's the request table — filters, model, route, latency distribution. I'm going to open a single request that had a 2.6s tail spike. note the top-level timeline, you'll see an initial model call, then a fallback call triggered.
[01:44] Tom: okay I see — that fallback shot looks like a smaller model, is that the auto-fallback policy?
[01:50] Jordan: exactly. In this case the policy was latency-first: if the primary model exceeds the 95th threshold, route to a lower-cost variant. you can configure thresholds and also warm KV cache settings.
[02:03] Leila: when you say "KV cache" are we talking about prefix caching or full KV cache for autoregressive sessions?
[02:09] Jordan: both. the console shows type: prefix and kv. prefix cache helps with repeated prompts, kv cache (the key-value attention cache) reduces token gen for streaming resumption. note here the hit ratio dips right before the spike.
[02:24] [00:02:30ish — automatic transcript garble: "K V cahc" in original audio]
[02:28] Tom: hmm that dip — could that be warm-start eviction during autoscale or is it a TTL?
[02:35] Jordan: great point — could be either. the trace details show node-level eviction events at 15:23:40, which correlates with an autoscale event. that autoscale temporarily recreated the worker and cache wasn't warmed.
[02:48] Samir: are these node events visible in our cloud logs or only in the console? we need them in our SIEM for audit.
[02:55] Jordan: by default audit logs include node lifecycle events; you can stream them to your cloud logging via the webhook / logging sink. we'll share the ingestion sample.
[03:07] Maya: just to flag — in enterprise Dedicated we can make hot-standby pools to avoid cold starts; that option will change cost/commit discussions.
[03:18] Leila: what's the typical delta in throughput when you turn on hot-standby?
[03:22] Jordan: depends on instance type but in our internal numbers you often see 30-60% fewer tail spikes for warm pools at about 8-12% additional reserved cost. we'll send the performance sheet.
[03:34] [03:45] Jordan: switching to trace playback — this is the neat part: you can play back the entire request across services, pause, expand spans, and jump to the exact token where the model hit an error or slow operation.
[03:52] Jordan: oh also note the request inspector has a preview of the prompt and the structured tool calls — obfuscated by default for privacy.
[04:05] Tom: can you show an example where the error isn't a model fallback but a malformed function call returned by the model — we had one of those last week.
[04:13] Jordan: yes — I have a trace for that. playing back now — you can see the function call span fail with a 4xx and a stacktrace from our reranker service. the console highlights the failing span and suggests probable causes: input schema mismatch, tool timeouts, or model hallucination.
[04:33] Leila: that's helpful. do you keep historical payloads for compliance? Samir: What about retention?
[04:40] Samir: yeah retention policy, and if we need to delete traces for GDPR requests how quick is that?
[04:45] Jordan: retention is configurable per-account. default hosted is 90 days, Dedicated you can request custom retention or export to your storage. deletion requests are processed within 48 hours and audit logged — we also provide a deletion webhook confirmation.
[04:58] [05:10] Maya: security note — we integrate with customer KMS for Private, and keys never leave the customer's environment. we'll drop the SOC2 summary and KMS integration doc after the call.
[05:21] Tom: please do. also, what's the granularity of RBAC in the console? we need role separation across SRE, Product, and SecOps.
[05:29] Jordan: RBAC is role-based plus route-level perms. you can scope a role to only view traces but not export or share links. SAML/SSO is supported with SCIM provisioning.
[05:40] Leila: practical question — if we want to reproduce a spike locally, can we export a replayable trace or script?
[05:47] Jordan: yes, there's an "export replay" option that gives a TAR with the request sequence and a simple runner script. you can replay against a sandbox or your dedicated endpoint.
[05:58] Tom: and that runner will respect kv-cache semantics? like it will warm the cache?
[06:03] Jordan: the runner includes an option to prepopulate the prefix cache or run cold to emulate first-time sessions. we'll attach a small example in the runbook.
[06:12] [06:30] Jordan: switching gears to error analysis — console surfaces the top error buckets, you can drill to user-agent, route, model variant. here's a histogram that shows model OOMs vs network timeouts. in our sample the spike was network queuing during autoscale.
[06:30] Tom: OOMs — are those mitigated by quantized models or by segmentation?
[06:36] Jordan: both can help. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles and model variant suggestions for your workload. for runtime we have soft-limit OOM handling and fallback to narrower context windows.
[06:50] Leila: could you show how the console surfaces an A/B rollout issue? like when we push canary and see errors only on canary.
[06:57] Jordan: sure — here we have a canary cohort filter. you can compare metrics side-by-side: token latency, error rate, cost. you can also auto-rollback the canary if error rate exceeds X for Y minutes.
[07:12] Samir: do those auto actions create a public audit trail? we need proof of changes for compliance audits.
[07:18] Jordan: yes — all rollouts, auto-rollbacks, and policy triggers are recorded in the audit log with actor and timestamp. you can export that log.
[07:28] [07:30] Leila: when we talk about model fallback, is context preserved or do you re-run from scratch?
[07:35] Jordan: when fallback happens during a streaming session, we try to reuse KV cache when compatible; otherwise we resubmit minimized context. we flag these in the trace so you can measure cost delta.
[07:48] Tom: could we get an alert when KV hit ratio drops below a threshold?
[07:53] Jordan: yes — alerting supports custom metrics including KV hit ratio. you can integrate with PagerDuty and Slack.
[08:00] [08:15] Jordan: demo: here's an example alert that triggered and the trace it linked to — open the trace, click "export replay", then toggle "pre-warm cache" and play.
[08:29] Tom: nice. that would speed troubleshooting a lot.
[08:33] Maya: quick commercial aside — for Dedicated with hot-standby the alert noise drops a lot, we can run a two-week pilot to quantify.
[08:42] Leila: cost is the main blocker for the execs — they want unit economics tied to accuracy.
[08:48] Maya: understood — we'll provide a cost/latency delta sheet and also a sample of Optimize recommendations for quantization and batching.
[08:58] [09:10] Jordan: last section — runbook walkthrough. first step: identify spike with request inspector, second: play trace and confirm the span that created the delay, third: check node events for recent autoscale or eviction, fourth: decide to warm cache or expand hot pool, fifth: if fallback induced lower quality, roll back. runbook includes command snippets to export traces and to trigger a manual warm.
[09:35] Leila: can you paste the runbook steps in a confluence-friendly format?
[09:39] Jordan: I'll send as markdown and a PDF — link in follow-up.
[09:43] Samir: are there any limitations with e2e tracing for multi-region traffic? we have EU and US endpoints and sometimes we see cross-region latencies.
[09:52] Jordan: traces include region tags and we surface inter-region hops. for strict data residency we can limit cross-region fallback in routing policies.
[10:05] Tom: perfect. ok can we talk about the forensic retention — if we need to keep a six month window for a specific route, how do we do that?
[10:12] Jordan: you can set per-route retention and also archive to your S3/GCS bucket. we'll include an example S3 lifecycle rule.
[10:20] Maya: we're going to share three artifacts: SOC2 summary, runbook + replay example, and the perf/cost delta spreadsheet. I'll send via the deal thread.
[10:29] Leila: thanks — also want that short screencap of the trace playback we saw.
[10:33] Jordan: will attach a 30s MP4.
[10:36] [10:40] Tom: one last question — if we onboard to Dedicated, how smooth is the migration for live traffic? can we do blue-green?
[10:46] Jordan: yes, we support blue-green and gradual traffic migration at the routing layer. you can bind a route to dedicated capacity and then shift traffic in increments. the console shows traffic split and rollback controls.
[10:59] Maya: ok, we're at time — quick recap of next steps and action items.
[11:05] Tom: thanks, this was useful. we'll collect the failing request IDs and send them.
[11:10] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the pilot.

References shared during call:
- Incident runbook (link): https://redwood.internal/runbooks/empiria-triage (placeholder)
